{{Short description|Mathematical theorem}}
{{for|the theorem in algebraic number theory|Bauer's theorem}}
In [[mathematics]], the '''Bauer–Fike theorem''' is a standard result in the [[perturbation theory]] of the [[eigenvalue]] of a complex-valued [[diagonalizable|diagonalizable matrix]]. In its substance, it states an absolute upper bound for the deviation of one perturbed matrix eigenvalue from a properly chosen eigenvalue of the exact matrix. Informally speaking, what it says is that ''the sensitivity of the eigenvalues is estimated by the condition number of the matrix of eigenvectors''.

The theorem was proved by [[Friedrich L. Bauer]] and C. T. Fike in 1960.

==The setup==
In what follows we assume that:
* {{math|''A'' ∈ '''C'''<sup>''n'',''n''</sup>}} is a [[diagonalizable|diagonalizable matrix]];
* {{math|''V'' ∈ '''C'''<sup>''n'',''n''</sup>}} is the non-singular [[eigenvector matrix]] such that {{math|''A'' {{=}} ''V''Λ''V''{{hairsp}}<sup>−1</sup>}}, where {{math|Λ}} is a diagonal matrix. 
* If {{math|''X'' ∈ '''C'''<sup>''n'',''n''</sup>}} is invertible, its [[condition number]] in [[matrix norm|{{mvar|p}}-norm]] is denoted by {{math|''κ<sub>p</sub>''(''X'')}} and defined by:
::<math>\kappa_p(X)=\|X\|_p \left \|X^{-1} \right \|_p.</math>

==The Bauer–Fike Theorem==
:'''Bauer–Fike Theorem.''' Let {{mvar|μ}} be an eigenvalue of {{math|''A'' + ''δA''}}. Then there exists {{math|''λ'' ∈ ''Λ''(''A'')}} such that:
::<math>|\lambda-\mu| \leq \kappa_p (V) \| \delta A \|_p</math>

'''Proof.''' We can suppose {{math|''μ'' ∉ ''Λ''(''A'')}}, otherwise take {{math|''λ'' {{=}} ''μ''}} and the result is trivially true since {{math|''κ<sub>p</sub>''(''V'') ≥ 1}}. Since {{mvar|μ}} is an eigenvalue of {{math|''A'' + ''δA''}}, we have {{math|det(''A'' + ''δA'' − ''μI'') {{=}} 0}} and so

:<math>\begin{align}
0 &= \det(A+\delta A-\mu I) \\
  &= \det(V^{-1})\det(A+\delta A-\mu I)\det(V) \\
  &= \det \left ( V^{-1} (A+\delta A-\mu I) V \right ) \\
  &= \det \left ( V^{-1}AV + V^{-1}\delta AV- V^{-1} \mu I V \right ) \\
  &= \det \left (\Lambda+V^{-1}\delta AV-\mu I \right ) \\
  &= \det(\Lambda-\mu I)\det \left ((\Lambda-\mu I)^{-1}V^{-1}\delta AV +I \right ) \\
\end{align}</math>

However our assumption, {{math|''μ'' ∉ ''Λ''(''A'')}}, implies that: {{math|det(Λ − ''μI'') ≠ 0}} and therefore we can write:

:<math>\det \left ((\Lambda-\mu I)^{-1}V^{-1}\delta AV +I \right ) = 0.</math>

This reveals {{math|−1}} to be an eigenvalue of 

:<math>(\Lambda-\mu I)^{-1}V^{-1}\delta AV.</math>

Since all {{mvar|p}}-norms are [[matrix norm|consistent matrix norms]] we have {{math|{{!}}''λ''{{!}} ≤ {{!!}}''A''{{!!}}<sub>''p''</sub>}} where {{mvar|λ}} is an eigenvalue of {{mvar|A}}. In this instance this gives us:

:<math>1 = |-1| \leq \left \|(\Lambda-\mu I)^{-1}V^{-1}\delta AV \right \|_p \leq \left \|(\Lambda-\mu I)^{-1} \right \|_p \left \|V^{-1}\right \|_p \|V\|_p\|\delta A\|_p = \left \|(\Lambda-\mu I)^{-1} \right \|_p\ \kappa_p(V)\|\delta A\|_p</math>

But {{math|(Λ − ''μI'')<sup>−1</sup>}} is a diagonal matrix, the {{mvar|p}}-norm of which is easily computed:

:<math>\left \| \left (\Lambda-\mu I \right )^{-1} \right \|_p\ =\max_{\|\boldsymbol{x}\|_p\ne 0} \frac{\left \|\left (\Lambda-\mu I \right )^{-1} \boldsymbol{x} \right \|_p}{\|\boldsymbol{x}\|_p} =\max_{\lambda\in\Lambda(A)}\frac{1}{|\lambda -\mu|}\ = \frac{1}{\min_{\lambda\in\Lambda(A)}|\lambda-\mu|}</math>

whence:

:<math>\min_{\lambda\in\Lambda(A)}|\lambda-\mu|\leq\ \kappa_p(V)\|\delta A\|_p.</math>

==An Alternate Formulation==
The theorem can also be reformulated to better suit numerical methods. In fact, dealing with real eigensystem problems, one often has an exact matrix {{mvar|A}}, but knows only an approximate eigenvalue-eigenvector couple, {{math|(''λ<sup>a</sup>'', '''''v'''<sup>a</sup>'')}} and needs to bound the error. The following version comes in help.

:'''Bauer–Fike Theorem (Alternate Formulation).''' Let {{math|(''λ<sup>a</sup>'', '''''v'''<sup>a</sup>'')}} be an approximate eigenvalue-eigenvector couple, and {{math|'''''r''''' {{=}} ''A'''v'''<sup>a</sup>'' − ''λ<sup>a</sup>'''v'''<sup>a</sup>''}}. Then there exists {{math|''λ'' ∈ ''Λ''(''A'')}} such that:
::<math> \left |\lambda-\lambda^a \right |\leq \kappa_p (V)\frac{\|\boldsymbol{r}\|_p}{\left \|\boldsymbol{v}^a \right \|_p}</math>

'''Proof.''' We can suppose {{math|''λ<sup>a</sup>'' ∉ ''Λ''(''A'')}}, otherwise take {{math|''λ'' {{=}} ''λ<sup>a</sup>''}} and the result is trivially true since {{math|''κ<sub>p</sub>''(''V'') ≥ 1}}. So {{math|(''A'' − ''λ<sup>a</sup>I'')<sup>−1</sup>}} exists, so we can write:

:<math>\boldsymbol{v}^a = \left (A-\lambda^a I \right )^{-1} \boldsymbol{r}= V \left (D-\lambda^a I \right )^{-1}V^{-1}\boldsymbol{r}</math>

since {{mvar|A}} is diagonalizable; taking the {{mvar|p}}-norm of both sides, we obtain:

:<math>\left \| \boldsymbol{v}^a \right \|_p= \left \|V \left (D-\lambda^a I \right )^{-1}V^{-1}\boldsymbol{r} \right \|_p \leq \|V\|_p \left \| \left (D-\lambda^a I \right )^{-1} \right \|_p \left \|V^{-1} \right \|_p \|\boldsymbol{r}\|_p =\kappa_p(V) \left \| \left (D-\lambda^a I \right )^{-1} \right \|_p \|\boldsymbol{r}\|_p.</math>

However 

:<math>\left (D- \lambda^a I \right )^{-1}</math> 

is a diagonal matrix and its {{mvar|p}}-norm is easily computed:

:<math>\left \|\left (D-\lambda^a I \right )^{-1} \right \|_p = \max_{\|\boldsymbol{x}\|_p \ne 0}\frac{\left \|\left (D-\lambda^a I \right )^{-1}\boldsymbol{x} \right \|_p}{\|\boldsymbol{x}\|_p} =\max_{\lambda\in\sigma(A)} \frac{1}{\left |\lambda-\lambda^a \right |}=\frac{1}{\min_{\lambda\in\sigma(A)} \left |\lambda- \lambda^a \right |}</math>

whence:

:<math>\min_{\lambda\in\lambda(A)} \left |\lambda-\lambda^a \right | \leq\kappa_p(V) \frac{\|\boldsymbol{r}\|_p}{\left \|\boldsymbol{v}^a \right \|_p}.</math>

==A Relative Bound==
Both formulations of Bauer–Fike theorem yield an absolute bound. The following corollary is useful whenever a relative bound is needed:

:'''Corollary.''' Suppose {{mvar|A}} is invertible and that {{mvar|μ}} is an eigenvalue of {{math|''A'' + ''δA''}}. Then there exists {{math|''λ'' ∈ ''Λ''(''A'')}} such that:
::<math>\frac{|\lambda-\mu|}{|\lambda|}\leq\kappa_p (V) \left \|A^{-1}\delta A \right \|_p</math>

'''Note.''' {{math|{{!!}}''A''<sup>−1</sup>''δA''{{!!}}}} can be formally viewed as the ''relative variation of'' {{mvar|A}}, just as {{math|{{sfrac|{{!}}''λ'' − ''μ''{{!}}|{{!}}''λ''{{!}}}}}} is the relative variation of {{mvar|λ}}.

'''Proof.''' Since {{mvar|μ}} is an eigenvalue of {{math|''A'' + ''δA''}} and {{math|det(''A'') ≠ 0}}, by multiplying by {{math|−''A''<sup>−1</sup>}} from left we have:

:<math>-A^{-1}(A+\delta A)\boldsymbol{v}=-\mu A^{-1}\boldsymbol{v}.</math>

If we set:

:<math>A^a =\mu A^{-1}, \qquad (\delta A)^a = -A^{-1}\delta A</math>

then we have:

:<math>\left (A^a + (\delta A)^a - I \right )\boldsymbol{v} = \boldsymbol{0}</math>

which means that {{math|1}} is an eigenvalue of {{math|''A<sup>a</sup>'' + (''δA'')<sup>''a''</sup>}}, with {{math|'''''v'''''}} as an eigenvector. Now, the eigenvalues of {{math|''A<sup>a</sup>''}} are {{math|{{sfrac|''μ''|''λ<sub>i</sub>''}}}}, while it has the same [[eigenvector matrix]] as {{mvar|A}}. Applying the Bauer–Fike theorem to {{math|''A<sup>a</sup>'' + (''δA'')<sup>''a''</sup>}} with eigenvalue {{math|1}}, gives us:

:<math>\min_{\lambda\in\Lambda(A)} \left|\frac{\mu}{\lambda}-1\right| = \min_{\lambda\in\Lambda(A)}\frac{|\lambda-\mu|}{|\lambda|} \leq \kappa_p (V) \left \|A^{-1}\delta A \right \|_p</math>

== The Case of Normal Matrices ==
If {{mvar|A}} is [[normal matrix|normal]], {{mvar|V}} is a [[unitary matrix]], therefore:

:<math>\|V\|_2= \left \|V^{-1} \right \|_2 = 1,</math>

so that {{math|''κ''<sub>2</sub>(''V'') {{=}} 1}}. The Bauer–Fike theorem then becomes:

:<math>\exists\lambda\in\Lambda(A): \quad  |\lambda-\mu|\leq\|\delta A\|_2</math>

Or in alternate formulation:

:<math>\exists\lambda\in\Lambda(A): \quad \left |\lambda-\lambda^a \right |\leq\frac{\|\boldsymbol{r}\|_2}{\left \|\boldsymbol{v}^a\right \|_2}</math>

which obviously remains true if {{mvar|A}} is a [[Hermitian matrix]]. In this case, however, a much stronger result holds, known as the [[Weyl's inequality|Weyl's theorem on eigenvalues]]. In the hermitian case one can also restate the Bauer–Fike theorem in the form that the map {{math|''A'' ↦ ''Λ''(''A'')}} that maps a matrix to its [[spectrum]] is a [[non-expansive function]] with respect to the [[Hausdorff distance]] on the set of compact subsets of {{math|'''C'''}}.
